lines.text: Three out of four animals in the open ocean can make their own light. Why?
Dive in, and sunlight fades fast. By two hundred metres, it's twilight. Below a thousand, it's night. Forever.
So life makes its own, by mixing a chemical fuel with an enzyme.
An anglerfish dangles a glowing lure. Something curious swims closer. Bad idea.
A hatchetfish lights up its belly to match the faint glow from above. Seen from below, its silhouette vanishes.
Grab certain jellyfish, and they flash like a burglar alarm, likely calling in something bigger to eat the attacker.
Most of this light is blue, because blue travels farthest in water. But one dragonfish cheats, with red light its prey can't see.
Sunlight never reaches most of the ocean. So its residents brought their own.
